title: Managing virtual appointments in chronic care
venue: IISE Transactions on Healthcare Systems Engineering
abstract: Virtual appointments between patients and healthcare providers can offer a cost-effective alternative to traditional office appointments for managing chronic conditions. Virtual appointments increase contact with the physician by either substituting or complementing office appointments, leading to improved health outcomes. The true value of virtual appointments cannot be realized until they are truly integrated with the office appointment systems. In this study, we introduce a capacity allocation model to study the use of virtual appointments in a chronic care setting. Specifically, we develop a finite horizon stochastic dynamic program to determine which patients to schedule for office and virtual appointments that maximizes aggregate health benefits across a cohort of patients. Optimal policy characterization for this problem is challenging. We find that, under certain conditions, a myopic heuristic, where the sickest patients are scheduled for office appointments and the next sickest patients are scheduled for virtual appointments, is optimal. We show that the myopic heuristic performs well even in more general settings. Our findings further show that virtual appointments serve a dual purpose: they may reduce the number of office appointments and may trigger follow-up office appointments.

summary.oneLiner: Scheduling the sickest patients for office visits and the next sickest for virtual visits is optimal under certain conditions, and performs well more generally.
summary.overview: Virtual appointments, such as video or phone consultations, can be a cheaper alternative to office visits for managing chronic conditions. The authors build a capacity allocation model that decides which patients should get office appointments and which should get virtual ones, with the aim of maximizing overall health benefits across a group of patients over a finite time horizon. Finding the best policy is hard, but the authors find that under certain conditions a simple rule works: give office visits to the sickest patients and virtual visits to the next sickest. They report that this rule performs well even in more general settings. The paper also suggests virtual appointments can both reduce the number of office visits and trigger follow-up office visits.
summary.question: How should a healthcare provider decide which chronic-care patients get office appointments and which get virtual appointments so as to maximize aggregate health benefits?
summary.method: The authors introduce a capacity allocation model, developed as a finite horizon stochastic dynamic program (a multi-period decision model that handles uncertainty over time). They characterize optimal policies, identify a myopic heuristic (a simple rule that decides period by period without looking ahead) and test how well it performs in more general settings.
